Making eye contact with other people
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner in this 34-year-old male unless there is unreported trauma content involving pregnancy, childbirth, or infants. The other trigger items point toward sexualized/interpersonal threat and hospital-associated reminders, making this item the clearest trauma-incongruent outlier.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeated lock-checking is more suggestive of fear of external intrusion/burglary than trauma-specific coping with partner physical abuse, and it is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The other maladaptive strategies reflect interpersonal avoidance and affect suppression, whereas this item introduces a different safety concern.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item duplicates compulsive checking behavior rather than describing a perceived current threat state, and it implies fear of break-in/external danger that is not otherwise supported by the trauma narrative, appraisals, or memory content. In combination with the matching maladaptive strategy item, it forms an internally coherent pair but one that is poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

vignette: Darius was thirty when the violence in the county hospital's East Wing did not end with a shout but with a heavy, familiar hand pressing him against the linoleum. He had been waiting for lab results when his partner arrived, and what started as a sharp exchange over missed payments swelled into physical force. The antiseptic sting of the floor cleaner clung to his clothes, the copper taste of a split lip bloomed across his tongue, and the muffled echo of the partner's voice seemed to hang in the sterile air long after the guard escorted them out. He is thirty-four now, and the memory does not sit in the past; when he pauses between files, he hears the exact cadence of the partner's words, tastes the iron again, and feels the weight of the floor against his shoulders as though the event is still unfolding. Over the following months, his body settled into a quiet readiness, running parallel to a constant mental sweep of the room. He walked through the parole office with his shoulders drawn up, perpetually braced, his gaze moving across parolees and clerks to catch any shift in posture or tone. When a male parolee was left alone with him in the consultation room, Darius felt the familiar tension rise, his muscles tightening as if waiting for the encounter to turn. He noticed how strangers' eyes lingered on him, and the sensation of being looked at sexually, particularly when the gaze carried a quiet, lingering quality, sent a familiar flutter of vulnerability through his chest. What frightened him most was not the stare itself, but the way it pulled him back to that hospital moment, when the world had narrowed to his body and the force against him. The habits formed gradually, woven into the rhythm of his days. He stopped meeting people's eyes, finding that direct gaze too exposed, and he folded quietly when disagreements arose over schedules, household decisions, or the quiet expectations of his relationship, avoiding escalation rather than risking it. Positive moments slipped through his fingers alongside the tension; a laugh shared with a coworker or a warm evening at home felt precarious, and he would gently pull away, convinced that letting himself rest in those feelings would only leave him open to being hurt again. The consequences of this quiet retreat accumulated steadily. His marriage grew distant as he maintained a careful neutrality, and at work he began declining home visits that required prolonged time alone with male parolees, citing paperwork backlogs while the knot in his stomach remained. A PCL5 score of 67 quantifies the heavy load he carries, though the number sits lightly beside the daily reality of his body on alert, scanning for danger, watching others. He had come to believe that his life had been quietly dismantled, not by a single catastrophic break but by a slow, steady unraveling. What had happened to him felt profoundly unfair; he had borne the weight of the violence while the years passed without acknowledgment, without restitution, and without the promise of safety. The injustice sat heavy in his chest, merging with a growing sense that life had lost its texture, leaving him uncertain whether he was living or merely enduring. At thirty-four, the days blurred into a routine of careful observation and restrained breath, but it was the accumulating weight of that hollow certainty that finally brought him to the clinic. He sits now on the edge of the examination chair, shoulders still set, hands resting lightly on his knees. He is afraid of the sudden flare of tension, of the world closing in again, but beneath the caution, he hopes that someone might finally help him untangle the past from the present, and teach him how to breathe without waiting for the next blow.
